passages.original: sed alio fortasse atque alio nomine ab aliis atque aliis nuncupatae sunt. Licet enim cuique rei incognitæ \ quæ nullum habeat usitatum nomen, quodlibet nomen imponere. Nam non est verisimile, sapientes aut nullos fuisse ante Platonem ; aut istas quas Plato, ut dictum est, ideas vocat, quæcumque res sint, non intellexisse : siquidem tanta in cis vis constituitur, ut nisi his intellectis sapiens esse nemo possit. Credibile est etiam præter Græciam fuissc in aliis genUbus sapientes : quod etiam Plato ipse non solum peregrinando eapienti perficiendæ gratia satis testatus est, sed etiam in iibris suis commemorat.
passages.english: but perhaps they were called by one name by some people and by another name by others. For it is permitted to give any name one likes to any unknown thing that has no customary name. For it is not likely that there were no wise men before Plato, or that they did not understand these things which Plato, as has been said, calls ideas, whatever these things may be; since so great a force is placed in them that no one can be wise unless they are understood. It is credible also that there were wise men in other nations besides Greece: Plato himself not only bore sufficient witness to this by travelling for the sake of perfecting [his] wisdom, but also mentions it in his books.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'cis' for 'eis', 'genUbus' for 'gentibus', 'eapienti' for 'sapientiae', 'iibris' for 'libris').

passages.original: Quod si hæ rerum omnium crcandarum creatarumve rationes in divina mente contineatur, neque in divina menle quidquam nisi æternum atquo incommutabile potest esse ; atque has rerum rationes principales appellat ideas Plato : non solum suut ideæ, sed ips:c veræ sunt, quia æternæ sunt, ct ejusmodi atque incommutabiles manent ; quarum participatione lit ut sit quidquid est, quoquomodo est. Sed anima rationalis inter eas res qua!
passages.english: But if these reasons of all things to be created or already created are contained in the divine mind, and nothing can be in the divine mind except what is eternal and unchangeable, and Plato calls these principal reasons of things ideas, then not only are there ideas, but they themselves are true, because they are eternal and remain of the same kind and unchangeable; and it is by participation in them that whatever exists comes to exist, in whatever way it exists.
